title: Himachali food: dham, siddu, trout and tea
meta_description: What to eat in Himachal: the dham feast, siddu, babru, chha gosht, Kinnaur's chilgoza and apples, Tibetan food in McLeodganj and Kangra tea, with prices.
summary: Himachali food is hill farm food: rajma, lentils, maize, buckwheat, yoghurt, ghee and seasonal greens, with feast cooking at weddings and fairs called dham. Eat siddu in Kullu, a dham in Kangra or Mandi, trout in Tirthan, chilgoza and apples in Kinnaur, and momos and thukpa in McLeodganj. Most of it costs ₹100–300 a plate.

sections.heading: What Himachalis actually eat
paras: Most visitors to Himachal eat café pasta and paneer butter masala and leave thinking the hills have no cuisine of their own. They do. Everyday food in a Himachali home is built on what the terraces grow: rajma and other beans, maize, wheat and rice in the lower valleys, buckwheat and barley higher up, with yoghurt, ghee and seasonal greens. Dishes are cooked slowly, often in yoghurt or with a little tamarind or dried mango for sourness, and spices are used with a lighter hand than in the plains.

Each part of the hive has its own habits. Kangra and Mandi are known for their feast cooking, Kullu for siddu and trout, Chamba for its lamb dishes and chilli sauce, and Kinnaur for its orchards, pine nuts and buckwheat. In McLeodganj, Bir and Manali, Tibetan families have added momos, thukpa and butter tea to the region's food since the 1960s. Ask your homestay what they cook at home: it is often not on any menu.

sections.heading: Dham: the feast on a leaf plate
paras: Dham is the festive meal of Himachal, served at weddings, temple fairs and family occasions. It is cooked by botis, hereditary cooks from Brahmin families, in large brass vessels over wood fires, and served by the ladle onto leaf plates called pattal to guests seated in rows on the floor. Each course arrives in a fixed order, and the food is vegetarian, made without onion and garlic.

The details change from district to district. A Kangra dham usually includes madra, a rich dish of chickpeas or beans cooked in yoghurt; dal of black gram; a sweet-and-sour khatta, often made with pumpkin or chickpeas; and sweet rice to finish. In Mandi, look for sepu badi, spinach cooked with dumplings of lentil paste. Chamba has its own madra and a famous sour dish of rajma or chickpeas.

You are most likely to eat dham at a festival such as Kullu Dussehra or the Minjar Mela, or as a guest at a family occasion. A few restaurants in Dharamshala, Mandi and Shimla serve dham on certain days; ask locally, as these change often. Eat with your right hand, accept second helpings, and do not leave until the row is finished.

sections.heading: Dishes to look for, and where
paras: These are dishes you can realistically find on a trip, at dhabas, homestays or festival stalls. Names and recipes vary between villages, and prices are indicative 2026 ranges.

sections.heading: Kullu, Chamba and the Tirthan valley
paras: In the Kullu valley, siddu is the dish to find. It is made from wheat dough left to rise, rolled around a filling of ground walnut, poppy seed or lentils, and steamed. Served hot with a spoon of ghee and green chutney, it is a winter food that is now sold all year at stalls in Manali, Naggar and Kullu. Small dhabas around the Mall and in Old Manali make it fresh; ask in the morning.

Chamba is known for chha gosht and for Chamba chukh, a fiery chilli sauce sold in jars in the bazaar, as well as for its dham. In the Tirthan valley and along the Beas, trout is the local speciality; homestays cook it fried or in a light curry, and fish farms supply restaurants across the valley. Fishing in the rivers needs a licence from the state fisheries department, so do not buy or catch wild fish without asking where it came from.

sections.heading: Kinnaur's orchards and pine nuts
paras: Kinnaur grows some of India's best apples. Many of the orchards trace back to the work of Satyananda Stokes, an American who introduced new apple varieties at Kotgarh near Narkanda in the early 20th century, after which apple growing spread across the upper Shimla hills and into Kinnaur. The harvest runs from about August to October, and in season you can buy boxes straight from growers along NH5.

The other Kinnauri treasure is chilgoza, the edible seed of the chilgoza pine that grows on the dry slopes around Kalpa and Reckong Peo. The cones are gathered in autumn, dried and opened, and the long, thin-shelled nuts are sold in Peo's market at prices that depend on the harvest. Higher villages grow buckwheat, used for rotis and pancakes, and families brew their own drinks for festivals; ask your homestay what is in season.
list: Buy apples from growers, not roadside resellers, for better prices.
Store chilgoza in a cool, dry bag; they spoil if kept damp.
Try buckwheat rotis or pancakes in a Kinnauri homestay.

sections.heading: How to eat well on the road
paras: The best Himachali meals rarely come from the places with the longest menus. On highways, look for dhabas where buses and trucks stop: the food turns over fast and the rajma, kadhi and rotis are made fresh through the day. In towns, the bazaar eateries near the bus stand feed local office workers and are cheaper and more local than the cafés on the Mall. In villages, your homestay kitchen is the restaurant, and dinner there is often the best meal of the trip.

A few habits help. Eat lunch as your main meal on long road days, when dhabas are busiest and freshest, and keep dinners light at height. Tell homestays early if you are vegetarian, vegan or avoid onion and garlic; most can adapt with notice. Carry a steel bottle and refill filtered water rather than buying plastic, which is hard to dispose of in the hills; Himachal has had a ban on some single-use plastics for years. Be ready for early closing: in small towns and villages, kitchens may shut by 9 pm.
list: Ask for the day's sabzi; it is usually seasonal and local
Try lassi or chaas with lunch to balance spicy dishes
Buy pickles, chutneys and dried fruit from cooperatives and growers
Leave no food packaging on trails or by rivers

sections.heading: Tibetan food and Kangra tea
paras: McLeodganj has the largest Tibetan community in India, and its cafés and family kitchens are the best place in the Himalaya outside Tibet to eat Tibetan food. Try steamed or fried momos, thukpa and thenthuk, hand-pulled noodle soups, and tingmo, a steamed bread. Butter tea, made with tea, salt and butter, is an acquired taste; try a small cup first. During Losar, families fry khapse biscuits.

Kangra tea has been grown on the slopes below the Dhauladhar since the mid-19th century and has a geographical indication tag. The industry was badly hit by the 1905 Kangra earthquake but survives in estates around Palampur and Dharamshala, producing green and black teas. Several estates and the cooperative in Palampur sell direct; a 100 g pack of good green tea costs a few hundred rupees.

faqs.q: What is the most famous food of Himachal Pradesh?
faqs.a: Dham, the feast cooked for weddings and festivals, is the signature of Himachali cooking, with madra, dal, khatta and sweet rice served on leaf plates. For everyday eating, siddu in Kullu and rajma-chawal at dhabas are the dishes most visitors remember.

faqs.q: Where can I eat a Himachali dham as a tourist?
faqs.a: The easiest way is at a temple fair or festival, such as Kullu Dussehra or Chamba's Minjar Mela. Some restaurants in Dharamshala, Mandi and Shimla serve dham on fixed days; ask locally, as these change. Homestays can sometimes arrange a small version with notice.

Much of it is, including the traditional dham. Meat dishes such as chha gosht in Chamba and trout in Kullu are popular too. Vegetarians eat very well in Himachal, and every dhaba has dal, rajma and seasonal vegetables.
Mostly mild to medium, flavoured with yoghurt, ghee and souring agents rather than heavy chilli. Chamba chukh, a chilli sauce, is the hot exception. Ask for less chilli if you need it.

faqs.q: Where can I try siddu in Manali?
faqs.a: Look for small stalls and dhabas around the Mall, the bus stand area and Old Manali, and in Naggar and Kullu. It is best fresh and hot in the morning or evening. A plate usually costs ₹80–200.

faqs.q: Where do I find the best momos in McLeodganj?
faqs.a: Family-run Tibetan cafés along Jogiwara Road, Temple Road and around the main square serve good momos and thukpa for ₹80–220. Small places with Tibetan families eating in them are usually the best sign.

faqs.q: When can I buy apples and chilgoza in Kinnaur?
faqs.a: Apples are harvested from about August to October and chilgoza is gathered in autumn, with fresh stock in Reckong Peo's market from October. Prices depend on the harvest; check before you buy in bulk.

faqs.q: Is it safe to eat street food in Himachal?
faqs.a: Generally yes at busy stalls and dhabas, where food is cooked fresh. Drink filtered or boiled water, avoid cut fruit left in the open, and choose places with steady customers.

faqs.q: Can I visit a tea garden in Kangra?
faqs.a: Yes. Estates around Palampur welcome visitors to walk through the gardens, and some offer tastings or factory visits in season. The Palampur cooperative tea factory sells direct. Check current status before you travel, as factory visits vary by season.
